lessons.title: Gaslighting: when your memory is the target
lessons.objective: Recognise gaslighting in two conversations, evaluate an alternative and apply the distinction to a new context.
lessons.teach:
Gaslighting is more than two people remembering a conversation differently. The concern is a repeated pattern in which one person undermines another's confidence in their perceptions or memory, especially when facts can be checked. Learn to identify attacks on credibility without treating every disagreement as abuse.

In this lesson, try to identify the action in the words, not the presumed diagnosis of the speaker. Each example is fictional, and several interpretations can remain plausible. The practice goal is to notice the exact shift in the conversation and decide what evidence or boundary would help next.
lessons.takeaway: Gaslighting is more than two people remembering a conversation differently. The concern is a repeated pattern in which one person undermines another's confidence in their perceptions or memory, especially when facts can be checked. Learn to identify attacks on credibility without treating every disagreement as abuse. People can misremember events or disagree sincerely. Look for repetition, power and whether a person will examine the evidence.

lessons.title: DARVO: reversing who must answer
lessons.objective: Recognise darvo in two conversations, evaluate an alternative and apply the distinction to a new context.
lessons.teach:
DARVO names a defensive sequence: deny the alleged action, attack the person raising it, then present the accused person as the real victim. Your task is to identify a shift away from an answerable allegation, without assuming that every denial or claim of being hurt is dishonest.

In this lesson, try to identify the action in the words, not the presumed diagnosis of the speaker. Each example is fictional, and several interpretations can remain plausible. The practice goal is to notice the exact shift in the conversation and decide what evidence or boundary would help next.
lessons.takeaway: DARVO names a defensive sequence: deny the alleged action, attack the person raising it, then present the accused person as the real victim. Your task is to identify a shift away from an answerable allegation, without assuming that every denial or claim of being hurt is dishonest. An accusation can genuinely be false. A person's distress may be real even while their response is evasive.

lessons.title: Blame shifting: whose choice was it?
lessons.objective: Recognise blame shifting in two conversations, evaluate an alternative and apply the distinction to a new context.
lessons.teach:
Blame shifting occurs when someone transfers responsibility for their voluntary conduct to somebody else. Provocation can explain why an interaction was difficult, but it does not make another person responsible for the speaker's threats, insults, lies or broken commitments.

In this lesson, try to identify the action in the words, not the presumed diagnosis of the speaker. Each example is fictional, and several interpretations can remain plausible. The practice goal is to notice the exact shift in the conversation and decide what evidence or boundary would help next.
lessons.takeaway: Blame shifting occurs when someone transfers responsibility for their voluntary conduct to somebody else. Provocation can explain why an interaction was difficult, but it does not make another person responsible for the speaker's threats, insults, lies or broken commitments. Context can be relevant to shared problems. Separating responsibility does not require deciding that only one person ever made mistakes.

lessons.title: Guilt pressure: when no becomes selfish
lessons.objective: Recognise guilt tripping in two conversations, evaluate an alternative and apply the distinction to a new context.
lessons.teach:

In this lesson, try to identify the action in the words, not the presumed diagnosis of the speaker. Each example is fictional, and several interpretations can remain plausible. The practice goal is to notice the exact shift in the conversation and decide what evidence or boundary would help next.

The key question is whether the request can be considered freely or whether disagreement will be treated as evidence of bad character. Care obligations can be real. Explaining a person's needs is not automatically manipulation.

lessons.title: Future promises: words versus follow-through
lessons.objective: Recognise future faking in two conversations, evaluate an alternative and apply the distinction to a new context.
lessons.teach:
Promises can be sincere. The phrase 'future faking' is commonly used when attractive future commitments repeatedly secure present concessions without concrete steps toward fulfilment. Do not infer deliberate deceit from one broken promise. Look for repetition, incentives and actual change.

In this lesson, try to identify the action in the words, not the presumed diagnosis of the speaker. Each example is fictional, and several interpretations can remain plausible. The practice goal is to notice the exact shift in the conversation and decide what evidence or boundary would help next.

Do not infer deliberate deceit from one broken promise. Look for repetition, incentives and actual change. Plans fail for ordinary reasons. Changed circumstances and honest renegotiation differ from using promises as leverage.

lessons.title: False dilemmas: the choice you were not offered
lessons.objective: Recognise false dilemma in two conversations, evaluate an alternative and apply the distinction to a new context.
lessons.teach:
A false dilemma presents two options as if they exhaust every possibility. In difficult conversations it can transform a reasonable request into a test of loyalty or love. The skill is to find legitimate missing options while accepting that some situations do involve real trade-offs.

The skill is to find legitimate missing options while accepting that some situations do involve real trade-offs. Some decisions genuinely have two available outcomes. Evaluate whether a third route is practicable, not merely imaginable.

lessons.title: Whataboutism: the detour away from a question

lessons.teach:
Whataboutism responds to a specific concern by introducing a different person's mistake or an unrelated grievance. The new concern might deserve attention, but it does not answer the first one. Learn to acknowledge a separate issue without letting it erase the original.

In this lesson, try to identify the action in the words, not the presumed diagnosis of the speaker. Each example is fictional, and several interpretations can remain plausible. The practice goal is to notice the exact shift in the conversation and decide what evidence or boundary would help next.

Comparisons can be relevant when testing consistency or equal treatment. The question is whether they clarify or merely evade.
